title: The Painted Confession Anew
premise: When Freya Zhou, archivist of St. Aldhelm's Cathedral, discovers that the diary of a woman missing for thirty years contains entries dated after her disappearance, the locked crypt beneath the cathedral becomes the center of a mystery the police never solved. Freya's quiet talent for reading what others overlook draws her into a web of alibis woven by the cathedral's founding families, who sealed the crypt to bury more than bones. As she deciphers the diary's coded marginalia, she realizes the missing woman, Elowen, may have staged her own death to survive someone inside the parish, and that the diary's final entry names her killer-to-be. The story ends when Freya lures the now-elderly murderer back to the crypt with a forged diary page, forcing a confession recorded by the cathedral's own acoustic arches, and Elowen, alive and hidden in plain sight as the cathedral's cleaning woman, finally reclaims her name.
about_author: Rosalind Thornbury is the pen name of a former parish archivist who spent a decade cataloguing cathedral records in the west of England before turning to fiction. Her mysteries are known for their reverence for documents, dust, and the quiet violence hidden in institutional memory.

chapters.title: The Fourth Accident
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. While re-cataloguing the cathedral's restricted archive, Freya notices that a fourth death—organist Peter Voss's fall down the crypt stairs—matches the pattern of three 'accidents' she quietly solved years ago. The crypt has been sealed since 1994, yet Voss's keys are missing. The emotional beat is unease: Freya's competence is also her isolation, and she realizes someone may be watching the archive the way she does.

chapters.title: Entries After the End
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Sorting Voss's effects, Freya finds a diary belonging to Elowen Pryce, a young woman who vanished in 1994. The final entries are dated weeks after her disappearance, in handwriting Freya verifies as Elowen's own. The beat is vertigo: the document that should end the mystery instead opens it, and Freya understands the police closed the wrong case thirty years ago.

chapters.title: The Founding Families
chapters.summary: Freya's POV, with an interpolated 1994 diary excerpt. Freya maps the parish's old families—the Ashcombes, the Reverend Hale, and the Vosses—whose donations built the cathedral and whose signatures authorized sealing the crypt. The diary hints Elowen worked for them all. The beat is claustrophobic belonging: Freya, an outsider hired to keep their records, begins reading the families as a single organism that protects itself.

chapters.title: Alibis Woven in Wool
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Interviewing the elderly survivors under the pretext of an archive exhibition, Freya collects alibis for the night Elowen disappeared—each one corroborated, each one suspiciously identical in phrasing, as if rehearsed. Detective Inspector Marsh, who once dismissed her, grudgingly reopens the file. The beat is the thrill of pattern-recognition curdling into fear: someone recognizes her questions for what they are.

chapters.title: What the Arches Heard
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Testing the cathedral's legendary acoustics for the exhibition, Freya discovers the whispering gallery above the crypt transmits sound perfectly to a hidden niche—meaning any confession made at the crypt door was audible to whoever waited there. The beat is revelation shadowed by dread: the architecture itself was a witness, and the diary's coded marginalia may be Elowen's transcript of what she overheard.

chapters.title: The Cleaning Woman's Eyes
chapters.summary: Alternating POV: Freya and Marta, the cathedral's silent cleaning woman. Freya notices Marta's intimate knowledge of spaces she shouldn't know—a locked sacristy, the crypt's secondary stair. Marta's chapters reveal she has watched Freya with desperate hope, recognizing in her the investigator Elowen once prayed for. The beat is a silent alliance forming across thirty years of performed invisibility.

chapters.title: The Price of the Alibi
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Freya cracks the marginalia code and reconstructs 1994: Elowen overheard the families planning to silence a whistleblower—her brother—and chose exile and a staged death over testimony that would have destroyed her too. Her survival cost her name, her history, everyone she loved. The beat is grief: Freya finally understands the theme that survival is never free, and that Elowen paid in identity.

chapters.title: Voss's Last Key
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Peter Voss wasn't investigating Elowen—he was her nephew, searching for proof his aunt lived, and someone killed him for getting close. Freya finds his key opens the crypt's secondary stair, and inside, evidence Elowen hid in 1994: letters, a bloodied cloth, and a list of names. The beat is escalation—the killer knows Freya has the list, and the cathedral closes early that night without explanation.

chapters.title: Confession in the Crypt
chapters.summary: Freya's POV, climax. Freya plants a forged final diary page naming the killer—Reverend Hale's son, now the cathedral's beloved benefactor—luring him to the crypt to destroy it. Confronted in the dark, he confesses to Voss's murder and to hunting Elowen in 1994, unaware the whispering gallery carries every word to DI Marsh waiting in the niche above. The beat is terror transfigured into triumph as the architecture itself becomes the trap.

chapters.title: A Name Reclaimed
chapters.summary: Freya's and Marta's POVs. In the aftermath, Marta stands before the parish and speaks as Elowen Pryce for the first time in thirty years, her testimony convicting the killer and unsealing the crypt at last. Freya, offered recognition she never sought, instead catalogs the recovered archive—and finds Elowen's final diary entry, addressed to whoever kept reading. The beat is belonging earned: two women who survived by disappearing finally take up space in the light.
